title: Editor overview
text: Level editor asge-editor is a native ImGui-based editor for authoring ASGE scenes visually: place and configure entities, wire up components, manage textures, animations and audio, and organise a project's scenes, without hand-writing TOML. It is a plain executable built from the same CMake tree as the engine. Native installers for Windows ( .exe ), Linux ( .deb ) and macOS ( .dmg ) ship with every tagged release: see Releases . Build from source build just the editor Copy cmake --preset windows-editor-debug cmake --build --preset windows-editor-debug --target asge-editor # binary lands at bin/Debug/asge-editor.exe The editor never links against or depends on Game / IGameState : it drives asge::ecs::Registry , SceneManager , AssetManager and IRenderer directly. See Getting Started for the full build setup. Guide Create a project Create or open a project and save its scenes from the File menu. Work with scenes Switch between a project's scenes, spot unsaved changes and rename a scene. Navigate the viewport Move entities, pan, zoom and set up the reference grid. Configure the game window Set the target game window size and preview what each camera frames. Add entities and components Create entities, edit their components in the Inspector and organise them in a hierarchy. Arrange the UI Create buttons, labels, checkboxes, sliders and panels and let a panel lay them out. Import and inspect assets Mount asset folders, load assets and preview them in the Asset Inspector. Add a collider Attach a Collider and draw its rect or circle directly on the viewport. Animate a sprite Slice a spritesheet into a clip and play it with an Animation component. Make an entity follow a path Author PathFollow waypoints by clicking on the viewport and preview the spline.

title: Create a project
text: Create a project A project is the durable unit; a scene is one of its levels. Everything project- and scene-related lives under the File menu. Steps Choose File → New → Create a Project... . Enter a name and a folder, the grid spacing and the game window size. Confirm. The editor creates the project and saves an Empty Scene inside it. Result: an .asgeproject file plus one .asgescene , both open in the editor. File menu reference Item What it does New → Create a Project... Name, folder, grid spacing and game window size; auto-creates and saves an "Empty Scene". New → Create a Scene... Adds a new scene to the current project (disabled without one). Save / Ctrl+P Saves only the project file (mounts, assets, view, scene list) - never scene data, even a dirty scene. Save As... Copies the project and every scene file to a new folder. Save Scene / Ctrl+S Saves the active scene's entities. Open... / Open Scene... Opens an existing .asgeproject / adds an existing .asgescene to the current project. Every scene-affecting item is disabled while no project is open, and scene-specific ones stay disabled until a scene is active: there is nowhere for a new entity or asset import to persist to otherwise. What is stored where .asgeproject - VFS mounts, known asset paths, view settings (grid spacing, target game window size) and the list of scene files. .asgescene - a plain TOML file with one level's entities, the same format SceneManager::SaveScene/LoadScene use anywhere in the engine. asge.session - remembers which project and scene were active; auto-saved every 30 seconds and restored on the next launch. It lives in your per-user data folder ( %APPDATA%\ASGE\Editor on Windows), not next to the executable, so it works when the editor is installed somewhere read-only such as C:\Program Files . Next: Work with scenes .

title: Work with scenes
text: Work with scenes A project can hold many scenes; the editor keeps exactly one active at a time. Steps Find the HUD panel next to the viewport's mouse-position readout. It shows Project: <name> and a Scene dropdown listing every scene the project knows about. Pick another scene. If the current one has unsaved changes (a filled dot next to the dropdown), it is saved first. To rename the active scene, use the Scene panel. This moves its .asgescene file on disk to match; no copy is left behind under the old name. Result: selection, dirty state and asset resolution are reset for the incoming scene. How switching works SceneManager keeps one scene's entities live at a time. Switching away suspends the outgoing scene into an in-memory snapshot instead of destroying it, and switching back to a visited scene restores that snapshot instead of re-reading from disk. Repeat switching is fast and a stale scene's entities never bleed into rendering, picking or the entity list. Previous: Create a project · Next: Navigate the viewport .

title: Navigate the viewport
text: Navigate the viewport The viewport is a real, resizable window with the engine's own camera and viewport math underneath, so every overlay pans and zooms exactly like the scene. Input Effect Left-drag Move the clicked entity (or drag a gizmo arm to constrain to one axis). Middle-drag Pan the camera. Scroll Zoom, anchored on the point under the cursor. Restore View Reset pan and zoom to the default. Set the grid spacing Open View → Grid (disabled without a project). Set the world-space spacing between the reference grid lines drawn behind every sprite. The value is saved in the project's own [View] settings, not in scene data. Previous: Work with scenes · Next: Configure the game window .

title: Configure the game window
text: Configure the game window Tell the editor what size a real build of the game runs at, so the previews match. Steps Open View → Game Window (disabled without a project). Set the target width and height. They are saved in the project's [View] settings. Previews Every entity with a Camera component gets a live preview box: a world-space rectangle showing exactly what that camera frames at the configured game window size, centred on the entity's visual midpoint (its sprite's bounds, not just its transform's corner) at that camera's zoom. It uses the same math as systems::CameraSystem at runtime but is never applied to the editor's own view. A separate preview anchored at the world origin shows the letterboxed game window itself, regardless of any camera, dimming everything outside it like a real letterbox. Previous: Navigate the viewport · Next: Add entities and components .

title: Add entities and components
text: Add entities and components Every entity in the active scene is listed on the right; click one, or click it in the viewport, to edit it live in the Inspector. Steps Click Create Entity in the Entities panel (or Create UI Element , see Arrange the UI ). Select it. The Inspector shows one collapsible section per component the entity has. Use Add Component to attach more. Edit fields directly: there is no intermediate copy and no Apply step. The trailing x on a section removes that component. Duplicate copies the entity with everything under it into the same parent; Delete removes just that entity and its children become roots. Component types A fixed, explicit set rather than generic reflection; each has a hand-written editor next to its Serializer<T> . Component Fields Name / Transform Display name; position, rotation, scale. Sprite Virtual texture path (picked from known assets, not typed), layer, Y-sort. Collider Rect or circle shape, drawable on the viewport: Add a collider . Camera Zoom and follow-smoothing; previewed live in the viewport. AudioSource Clip path (picked from known audio), volume, loop. Animation Clip path, frame duration and a Play/Stop button. It starts stopped so nothing auto-plays when added. PathFollow Waypoints authored on the viewport: Make an entity follow a path . Velocity / Rigidbody Plain physics data: linear velocity, mass and drag. RenderInfo Layer, Y-sort, screen space and sort inheritance. Added automatically, once, whenever a Sprite is. UI components UIRect, UIButton, UILabel, UICheckbox, UISlider, UIPanel and UILayoutItem. Parent entities The Entities panel is a tree: roots at the top level, children nested behind a collapsible arrow. A selected child shows a read-only Parent line. A child's transform is relative to its parent, so moving the parent moves everything under it. title: Arrange the UI
text: Arrange the UI Build HUDs and menus without writing TOML. Widgets are assembled through the same ui::Create* functions a game uses, so what you see is what a game gets. Create a widget Click Create UI Element in the Entities panel (disabled until a project is open). Pick a type, then fill in its details. Back returns to the type list; Discard closes without creating. In the Panel Parent section at the end of every form, choose a panel (default (none) ) to create the widget as that panel's child. A panel can parent another panel, which is how you nest layouts. Type Settings Button Name, position, size, enabled flag, Color / Hover / Pressed colours, optional caption. Label Text, font, size, alignment and colour. Auto Size fits the rect to the text; turn it off for a fixed size. Checkbox Box colours, the check colour and whether it starts checked. Slider Min, Max and starting Value, the track colour and the thumb's Color / Hover / Pressed colours. Panel Background and border colours, margin, padding, spacing and a layout for its children. Every type also takes a Name, a Position and a Screen Space flag (on by default, so HUD elements stay put while the viewport pans and zooms). Fonts are picked from those loaded in the Assets panel. Afterwards each widget's components appear as Inspector sections (UIRect, Interactable, UIButton, UILabel, UICheckbox, UISlider, UIPanel) without an x : delete the whole entity instead. You can also drag an entity's row onto a panel in the Entities tree to move it in later. Panel layouts A panel's Layout decides where its children go, applied live in the viewport. Layout Behaviour Absolute Children keep whatever position and size they have. Grid (Rows, Columns) Equal cells, filled row by row in sibling order. VStack (Rows) Equal-height rows, each as wide as the panel, top to bottom. HStack (Columns) Equal-width columns, each as tall as the panel, left to right. Slots sit inside the panel's rect, inset by its Margin and Padding, with Spacing

title: Import and inspect assets
text: Import and inspect assets Assets are addressed by virtual path everywhere in ASGE. The editor gives you a panel for the mounts that back those paths and one for browsing what they resolve to. Steps In the Virtual File System panel, add a mount (a virtual root pointing at a real directory) with the native folder picker. In the Assets panel, use Load Asset... to bring in a texture, animation clip, audio clip or .ttf font. The panel lists everything the editor knows about: assets some entity references, plus those you loaded explicitly (so an unused import still shows up). Click an entry to open the Asset Inspector : absolute path, mountpoint and file size, plus a preview for the kind. Kind Preview Texture Pixel dimensions and a scaled thumbnail. Audio clip Duration, size, and working Play/Pause and Rewind controls. Animation clip Every FrameTable field plus a live, cycling preview of its sliced frames. Font A sample string rendered with the font's own glyph metrics. Fonts feed a label's Font Path; changing a label's font size re-bakes it. Next: Animate a sprite turns a spritesheet texture into a playable clip.

title: Add a collider
text: Add a collider Collider shapes get their own viewport interaction mode instead of raw number fields. Steps Select an entity and add a Collider from Add Component . Pick the shape in the Collider Shape dropdown ( Rect or Circle , default Rect). The editor remembers each shape's own last dimensions per entity, so switching back and forth loses neither. Click Draw Collider , then press to anchor the shape and drag to grow it: a rect defines opposite corners, a circle's drag sets its radius from the anchor. Release to commit; Esc restores the previous shape. Reset Collider zeroes the current shape's dimensions. Drawing edits the live Collider component, so the translucent overlay every collider already has shows it updating in real time. Previous: Arrange the UI · Next: Animate a sprite .

title: Animate a sprite
text: Animate a sprite Turn a spritesheet into something an Animation component can play, without an external tool or hand-written TOML. Steps Open the spritesheet texture in the Asset Inspector and click Create Clip . In the modal, set Rows and Columns . A bigger thumbnail shows a live grid overlay and the computed per-cell pixel size. Click Apply . The editor writes <image>_clip.toml next to the texture (creating or overwriting it), then registers and selects it as a new animation clip. Add an Animation component to an entity, choose the clip path and frame duration, and press Play . A clip records which texture it slices ( m_OriginAsset ), so once one exists the texture's button becomes Open Clip and jumps straight to it. Importing a .toml by hand via Load Asset... that doesn't identify its own texture this way is rejected rather than imported half-configured. Previous: Add a collider · Next: Make an entity follow a path .

title: Make an entity follow a path
text: Make an entity follow a path A PathFollow's waypoints are placed on the viewport rather than typed as numbers. Steps Add a PathFollow component to the entity. Click Select Waypoints in its Inspector section. The viewport becomes a click-to-place surface. Edit the path with the mouse, then click End Selection to commit and leave the mode. Input Effect Click Append a waypoint at the cursor's world position. Drag a point Move it (a fixed screen-pixel pick radius, so it is grabbable at any zoom). Right-click a point Remove it. Esc Discard everything placed this session, restoring what was there before. End Selection Commit and exit the mode. Waypoints stay visible as pin markers after selection ends. Outside edit mode, a real Catmull-Rom curve, the same interpolation PathFollowingSystem uses at runtime, overlays the straight point-to-point lines, sampled at the component's own Resolution , so it previews the path the entity will actually follow. Previous: Animate a sprite .

title: Getting Started
text: Installation Build ASGE from source ASGE builds a static library target and installs a CMake package config, so it can be consumed as a subdirectory, via FetchContent , or as an installed package. Prerequisites A C++23 compiler — MSVC on Windows, GCC/Clang on Linux, Clang on macOS CMake ≥ 3.31 Git Clone the repository shell Copy git clone https://github.com/lmriccardo/a-simple-game-engine.git asge cd asge Fetch vendored dependencies SDL3 and the stb single-header libraries aren't pulled in by CMake — a script vendors them per platform. Windows (PowerShell) Linux / macOS Windows (PowerShell) Copy ./scripts/install-deps.ps1 Linux / macOS Copy ./scripts/install-deps.sh Configure, build and test Using one of the provided CMake presets (also buildable without a preset via plain cmake -S . -B build ): Windows Linux macOS Windows Copy cmake --preset windows cmake --build --preset windows ctest --preset windows-debug Linux Copy cmake --preset linux cmake --build --preset linux ctest --preset linux-debug macOS Copy cmake --preset macos cmake --build --preset macos ctest --preset macos-debug Built examples land in bin/ . Using ASGE in your own C++ project Either way, pull in the whole engine through the umbrella header: Copy #include <ASGE/ASGE.hpp> Option 1 — add_subdirectory Vendor ASGE into your project (e.g. as a submodule under third-party/asge ) and add it directly: CMakeLists.txt Copy add_subdirectory(third-party/asge) add_executable(my_game main.cpp) target_link_libraries(my_game PRIVATE ASGE) # On Windows, my_game.exe also needs SDL3.dll next to it at runtime asge_copy_sdl3_runtime(my_game) Option 2 — FetchContent CMakeLists.txt Copy include(FetchContent) FetchContent_Declare( asge GIT_REPOSITORY https://github.com/lmriccardo/a-simple-game-engine.git GIT_TAG main SOURCE_DIR "${CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR}/third-party/asge" ) FetchContent_MakeAvailable(asge) add_executable(my_game main.cpp) target_link_libraries(my_game PRIVATE ASGE) asge_copy_sdl3_runtime(my_game) ASGE's own de

title: A Simple Game Engine
text: A Simple Game Engine · ASGE ASGE Overview Engine Editor Releases GitHub Search Ctrl K Overview Engine Editor Releases GitHub MIT Licensed · C++23 · SDL3 A Simple Game Engine, built to stay out of your way. ASGE is a modular, lightweight, cross-platform 2D game engine written in modern C++ (C++23) on top of SDL3 . Small composable subsystems, an ECS-based gameplay layer, and a growing set of runnable examples — targeting Windows, Linux and macOS. Get started Browse examples API reference View on GitHub 20 runnable examples C++23 modern, header-driven API 3 target platforms SDL3 current render backend Engine Install ASGE, learn how it works, browse the API reference and runnable examples. Level editor Build projects, scenes, colliders and animations visually, then run them on the engine. Built around four ideas Performance Thin abstractions over SDL3, custom allocators, and a thread pool for concurrent work — the engine tries to stay out of your frame budget's way. Simplicity Small, composable subsystems instead of one monolithic framework. Pull in what a game needs through the ASGE.hpp umbrella header. Extensibility An ECS-based gameplay layer plus a signal/event system ( asge::signals::Signal ) for decoupling systems from each other. Tooling A debug logger, timing/profiling utilities ( ScopedTimer ), a virtual filesystem, and a growing set of runnable examples. title: Engine theory
text: Engine theory What the main parts of a game engine do, and how ASGE implements each one. Every page first explains the concept, then shows the ASGE types that realise it, with a short snippet. Entity-Component-System Why a game object is split into identity, data and behaviour, and how ASGE's Registry stores entities and components, iterates them through views, and runs systems over them each frame. Game loop & timing How the main loop reads input, updates the simulation with a delta time and renders, the order in which systems run every frame, and how game states, the clock and the profiler fit around it. Events & signals How raw SDL events are translated into engine events, and how the type-safe Signal/Connection pattern lets one part of the program announce something without knowing who is listening. Memory & threading The custom allocators (linear, pool, stack and free-list) that avoid per-frame heap traffic, when each one fits, and how the ThreadPool spreads work across cores. Input How raw keyboard and mouse events become the questions gameplay code asks, such as whether a key is down, was just pressed or was just released, and how the per-frame input state is kept and queried. Rendering The thin rendering layer over SDL3: the VideoSystem and window, the abstract IRenderer, textures and sprites, cameras, and how draw calls reach the backend each frame. Audio How ASGE opens the audio device and mixes several clips at once through a pool of streams, and how AudioSource components and the AudioSystem drive playback from the scene. Filesystem & VFS How virtual paths are mounted onto real directories so game data does not depend on where it lives, plus the file IO helpers and the file watcher used to detect changes on disk. Assets How the AssetManager loads each file once and caches it by virtual path, how sprites are resolved into textures, and how spritesheet frame tables describe animation frames. Scenes How a level's entities are saved to a scene file and loade

title: Entity-Component-System
text: Entity-Component-System An ECS splits a game object into identity , data and behaviour , so behaviour can be written once and applied to every object that has the right data. The concept Entity - just an id. It carries no data and no code. Component - a plain bundle of data (a position, a sprite, a collider) attached to an entity. System - a function that walks every entity owning a given set of components and acts on them. Storing each component type in its own densely packed array keeps iteration cache-friendly, and composing objects from components avoids deep inheritance hierarchies. Why not inheritance? The classic alternative is a class tree: Enemy derives from Actor , a flying enemy from Enemy , and so on. It works until a new object needs a mix of branches (a flying, shooting, destructible crate) and the tree has to be reshuffled. With components, that crate is just an entity carrying the right bundle of data; no class had to change. Data-oriented layout CPUs are fast at reading memory in order and slow at chasing pointers. A system that touches only Position and Velocity reads two tightly packed arrays and never loads the sprite, health or audio data of the same entities. That is the main performance argument for an ECS, and it grows with the entity count. Systems and ordering Systems hold no state of their own; everything they need is in components or shared resources. That makes them easy to test and to reason about, but it means order matters: gravity must run before movement, and movement before collision, or objects react to last frame's positions. Engines therefore fix the system order in one place. Trade-offs The price is indirection. Finding "the one entity with component X" means a lookup, behaviour is spread across systems instead of living in one class, and removing an entity while iterating needs care. For small, singular objects (the player controller, say) plain code is often clearer; the ECS earns its keep for the many similar things in a sce

title: Game loop & timing
text: Game loop & timing The game loop is the heartbeat of a game: read input, advance the simulation by the time that passed, draw, repeat. The concept Each iteration of the loop is a frame . Simulation code must be told how long the previous frame took (the delta time ) so movement stays the same speed on a 30 Hz and a 144 Hz display. Engines differ on whether the simulation uses a variable step (one update per frame with the real delta) or a fixed step (update at a constant rate, possibly several times per frame); a variable step is simpler, a fixed step is more deterministic. Anatomy of a frame Every frame does the same four jobs in the same order: input (drain the OS event queue and update input state), update (advance the simulation), render (draw the result) and present (swap the finished image onto the screen). Doing input first means the update sees the freshest state; presenting last is what makes a frame visible at all. Delta time Without delta time, x += 5 each frame moves twice as far at 120 FPS as at 60 FPS. Multiplying by the seconds since the last frame, x += speed * dt , makes motion depend on time and not on frame rate. A very long frame (a breakpoint, a window drag) produces a huge delta that can push objects through walls, which is why engines often clamp it. Variable versus fixed step A variable step is the simplest option and fine for most games. A fixed step runs the simulation at a constant rate (say 60 times a second) and accumulates leftover real time, so results are reproducible and physics stays stable; the cost is more machinery, and rendering then often needs to interpolate between two simulation states. Pacing the frame Without a limit a loop runs as fast as the machine allows, burning CPU and battery for no visible gain. Engines either wait for the display's vertical sync or sleep until the target frame time has passed. Time can also be scaled (slow motion) or paused, which is why a clock distinguishes scaled game time from unscaled real ti

title: Events & signals
text: Events & signals Decoupled communication lets one part of the program announce that something happened without knowing who cares. The concept Two common patterns: an event stream , where the platform produces a sequence of typed messages that code polls or receives, and signals and slots , where a producer exposes a typed signal and any number of listeners (slots) connect callbacks to it. Both remove direct dependencies between the sender and its receivers. Why decouple? If the player code calls the HUD directly, the player depends on the HUD, and the HUD cannot be removed or tested without it. With an announcement instead ("score changed"), the producer neither knows nor cares who listens: the HUD, an achievement tracker and a sound effect can all react, and none of them is named in the player code. Polling versus callbacks An event stream is usually pulled : the loop drains a queue once per frame and handles each message in order, so all reactions happen at a predictable point. A signal is pushed : the slots run immediately, inside the call that emitted it. Push is convenient but means arbitrary code runs in the middle of the emitter's work, so a slot that modifies the very collection being iterated can cause trouble. Lifetimes The classic bug of callbacks is the dangling listener: an object is destroyed but its callback is still registered, and the next emit calls into freed memory. Any signal design therefore needs a way to disconnect, either explicitly or automatically when the listener goes away. How ASGE does it System events SDL events are translated once, in event::_internal::ProcessEvent , into asge::event::SystemEvent : a std::variant over QuitEvent , WindowEvent , KeyboardEvent , MouseMotionEvent , MouseButtonEvent , MouseWheelEvent and UnknownEvent . Game code never sees SDL types; it asks for the case it cares about with TryGet<EventT>() , which returns a pointer or null. Application forwards each event to the input system and then to Game::OnSystemEve

title: Memory & threading
text: Memory & threading Games allocate and free a lot of small things every frame; predictable allocation and safe parallel work keep the frame time steady. The concept General-purpose new / delete can be slow and fragment memory. Game engines replace it, where it matters, with allocators that match an allocation pattern : bump pointers for per-frame scratch data, pools for many same-sized objects, stacks for strictly nested lifetimes. For CPU parallelism, a thread pool reuses a fixed set of worker threads instead of spawning one per task. Why general allocation hurts A general-purpose allocator has to handle any size and any lifetime, so it searches for free blocks, takes locks in multithreaded programs and leaves gaps behind as blocks of different sizes come and go ( fragmentation ). Its cost is also unpredictable, which shows up as an occasional slow frame. Knowing the allocation pattern lets you replace all that with a few instructions. Matching pattern to allocator A linear (arena) allocator just bumps a pointer and frees everything at once: ideal for scratch data that dies at the end of a frame. A pool keeps same-sized slots on a free list: ideal for many identical objects that come and go in any order. A stack allows frees only in reverse order, matching strictly nested lifetimes. The restriction is the point; each gives up some flexibility in exchange for speed and predictability. Threads in a game Creating a thread costs far more than calling a function, so spawning one per small task loses the benefit. A thread pool starts its workers once and feeds them jobs from a queue. The hard part of parallel code is not starting work but sharing data safely: jobs should either own their data or touch disjoint parts of it, since locks reintroduce the stalls parallelism was meant to remove. How ASGE does it Allocators ( asge::mem ) Type Pattern Notes LinearAllocator Arena / bump pointer O(1) alloc over a buffer you provide; Reset() frees everything, GetMarker() + Rewind()

title: Input
text: Input Input turns raw key and mouse events into answers to the questions gameplay code actually asks: is it held, did it just go down, how far did the mouse move. The concept The OS reports events ("key down", "key up"); a game wants state . Engines keep two snapshots, the current and the previous frame, and derive three queries from them: down (held now), pressed (up last frame, down now) and released (down last frame, up now). Edge queries such as "pressed" are what make a jump fire once instead of every frame the key is held. Why snapshots? Reacting to events directly ("on key down, jump") scatters input handling across the code and makes it hard to ask state questions such as "is the player holding right?". Polling a per-frame snapshot gives every system one consistent answer for the whole frame, no matter how many events arrived or in what order, and keeps input code in the update step where gameplay logic lives. Mouse input The mouse adds continuous values: a position (where the pointer is now), a delta (how far it moved this frame) and a scroll amount. Positions are in window space, so converting to world coordinates is the camera's job. Deltas and scroll must be accumulated across all events in a frame and reset on the next one, otherwise several small motions in one frame are lost. Keys, not characters Game controls care about physical keys (a "move left" binding), not the text the key would type. That is why input is expressed in key codes; remapping then means changing a binding instead of rewriting logic. How ASGE does it asge::input::InputSystem is owned by Application and mirrors VideoSystem 's shape. Every frame the loop calls NewFrame() to roll the current snapshot into the previous one, then feeds each polled SystemEvent through ProcessEvent() (see Events & signals ). It is not a second event source: InputState simply consumes the same stream that also reaches Game::OnSystemEvent . Games never touch the system. Each state's Update receives a read-on

title: Rendering
text: Rendering Rendering gets pixels onto a window. ASGE keeps this layer thin: an abstract renderer, a window and a texture, with SDL3 as the only backend today. The concept A 2D renderer exposes a small drawing vocabulary (clear, shapes, textures, text) and a way to present the finished frame. Hiding it behind an interface keeps game code independent of the graphics API, so a different backend could be added later without touching gameplay. Cameras convert world space (where things are in the level) into screen space (pixels in the window). Immediate versus retained An immediate-mode renderer draws what you tell it to, right now, every frame; nothing is remembered between frames. A retained scene graph keeps objects and draws them for you. Immediate mode is simple and fits 2D games where the scene is already stored elsewhere (here, in the ECS); the cost is that you submit every draw call yourself each frame. Textures and the GPU An image decoded in RAM must be uploaded to the GPU before it can be drawn quickly. Uploading is slow, so it should happen once and the resulting texture be reused, which is the reason textures are cached by the asset layer. Draw order also matters in 2D: later draws cover earlier ones, so sprites are sorted by layer (and often by their Y position for a top-down look) before submission. Cameras A camera is a position and a zoom. Subtracting its position and scaling by the zoom maps a world coordinate onto the window, and the inverse maps a mouse click back into the world. The same transform lets the renderer skip anything outside the visible area ( culling ), which saves draw calls in large levels. How ASGE does it Video system and backends asge::video::VideoSystem brings up a window and a renderer for a chosen GraphicsBackend through a factory and hands them out as IWindow& and IRenderer& . Only GraphicsBackend::SDL exists; OpenGL, Vulkan and DirectX are future possibilities, which is why everything above this layer talks to the interfaces. IR

title: Audio
text: Audio Audio plays sound clips on the machine's output device, several at once, driven by components on entities. The concept A game needs many sounds playing concurrently, each with its own volume and looping, without allocating while the game runs. Engines open one output device, keep a bounded pool of streams bound to it, and feed decoded clip data into those streams. Decoded sound Audio on a computer is a long run of numbers, samples , played at a fixed rate (for example 44,100 per second). A clip is decoded once into that raw form; playing it means copying samples to the device just ahead of the speaker. If the copying is late the sound crackles, which is why audio must never wait on slow work such as loading a file. Mixing Speakers receive one signal, so several sounds are mixed by adding their samples together, each scaled by its own volume ( gain ). Too many loud sounds at once can exceed the maximum and distort, so engines cap the number of simultaneous voices; a bounded pool also keeps memory use predictable. Sound as game state Treating a sound as something an entity has (play, stop, loop) rather than a one-off call means it can be saved in a scene, edited in a tool and driven by the same systems as everything else. The system, not gameplay code, owns the details of starting and stopping streams. How ASGE does it AudioDevice and AudioStream asge::audio::AudioDevice owns SDL's audio subsystem, one physical playback device and a fixed pool of 32 AudioStream s. Initialize() opens the default device; CreateStream(AudioClip&) returns a std::shared_ptr<AudioStream> matching the clip's format, and DetachStream() gives the slot back. SetGain() sets the device volume. An AudioStream wraps one SDL_AudioStream : PutData() queues a clip, ClearData() empties it, SetAudioGain() sets its own volume. The shared pointer stays valid even if another detach relocates its slot. Application initializes the device alongside the video system and passes it into your game. AudioSou

title: Filesystem & VFS
text: Filesystem & VFS Assets are referred to by virtual paths, so a game's data does not depend on where it is installed. The concept Hard-coding C:\Users\me\game\hero.png breaks the moment the game moves. A virtual file system maps short, stable names ( textures/hero.png ) onto real directories chosen at startup. The same game data then works from a dev checkout, an installed build or an archive, and tools can remap folders without touching scenes. Mounts The usual model is the mount : a virtual root such as textures is bound to a real folder. Looking up a virtual path replaces the root with the real folder, so only the mount table needs to know where data really lives. With several mounts you can layer a mod folder over the base game, as the first match wins. Why not relative paths? Relative paths depend on the working directory , which changes with how the game is launched (double click, terminal, IDE). Absolute paths bake in a developer's machine. Virtual paths avoid both and also use forward slashes everywhere, so scene files behave the same on Windows, Linux and macOS. Watching files Tools want to react when a file changes on disk, for example reloading a texture after an artist saves it. Operating systems offer native notifications for this, which are cheaper and faster than re-scanning folders. The watcher runs on its own thread so waiting for changes never blocks the game. How ASGE does it VirtualFileSystem asge::filesystem::VirtualFileSystem keeps a list of mounts , each binding a virtual root to a real directory: Mount(root, realPath) and Unmount() manage bindings; a root can be mounted more than once. Resolve(virtualPath) returns the real Path , trying each mount whose root prefixes the path in registration order. Exists() , IsMounted() , ListMounts() and SplitRoot() inspect state. ToVirtualPath(realPath) goes the other way, which the editor uses when you pick a file on disk. Paths are normalized before use, and fallible calls return Result / BoolResult inste

title: Assets
text: Assets Loading an image or a sound is slow; loading it twice is wasteful. An asset layer loads each file once and shares it. The concept Assets (textures, fonts, audio, animation data) are loaded by name and cached, so the second request for the same asset is a lookup. Components then hold a cheap reference or a path instead of a copy, and a scene file can store just the path. Caching and sharing If a hundred enemies use the same sprite sheet, loading it a hundred times wastes time and memory. A cache keyed by path returns the same loaded asset to everyone. Shared ownership means the asset stays alive while anything uses it and can be freed once nothing does. Handles instead of data Components that store the loaded data itself cannot be saved to a file, and are expensive to copy. Storing the path (or a small handle) keeps components light and saveable; a separate step later turns the path into the live resource. That resolve step is where a missing or broken file is detected and reported. Loading cost Decoding an image or sound, then uploading it to the GPU, can take milliseconds, enough to drop frames. Engines load at well-chosen moments (between levels, behind a loading screen) or in the background. Parameters that change the result, such as a font's pixel size, must be part of the cache key, since the same file at two sizes is two different assets. How ASGE does it AssetManager and AssetPool asset::AssetManager is the one entry point. It is built over a VirtualFileSystem and owns a path-keyed AssetPool per asset type, each a cache of std::shared_ptr<Asset<T>> : GetImage , GetAudio , GetFrameTable by virtual path; GetFont by path and pixel height, since a font is baked at a size. GetTexture uploads an image to the GPU once, caches the ITexture by virtual path and keeps ownership; UnloadTexture drops it. Loads fail with a Result error when the path does not resolve through the VFS or the file cannot be decoded. assets.cpp Copy asge::game::asset::AssetManager assets

title: Scenes
text: Scenes A scene is one level's worth of entities, saved to a file and loaded back. The concept Because an ECS world is just entities and plain-data components, a level can be serialized by writing out every entity's components and rebuilt by reading them back. That makes levels data rather than code, and lets tools such as the level editor author them. A scene manager decides which scene is active and how to switch between them. What a scene contains A scene stores what is needed to rebuild the world : entities and the plain data of their components, with references to other things (assets, parent entities) written as stable names instead of memory addresses. Runtime-only state, such as a loaded texture, is not saved but rebuilt on load from those names. Identity across save and load Entity ids are only meaningful inside one running program. When a scene is loaded, new entities get new ids, so anything that refers to another entity (a parent link, say) must be translated from the saved reference to the new one. Getting this remapping right is the hardest part of any serializer. Switching scenes Switching can mean destroying the old world and loading the new from disk, which is simple but slow, or keeping visited scenes in memory so returning is instant at the cost of RAM. Which is right depends on how big levels are and how often players move between them. How ASGE does it SceneSerializer SceneSerializer writes every alive entity of a Registry to a TOML scene file ( .asgescene ) and populates a registry from one. Each component type has its own Serializer<T> specialization. Asset references are stored as virtual paths, which is why scenes survive being moved: see Filesystem & VFS . SceneManager SceneManager owns one Registry holding only the active scene's entities. LoadScene(virtualPath) makes a scene active, SaveScene(path) saves the active one, UnloadScene() clears it and RenameActiveScene() retags it for "Save As". title: Physics
text: Physics 2D physics here means three things: moving things, noticing when they overlap, and deciding what happens next. The concept A simple engine splits collision into a broad step (which pairs might touch), a narrow step (do these two shapes overlap, and by how much) and resolution (push them apart, or just report it). Shapes carry a layer and a mask so, for example, bullets can ignore other bullets. Why a broad phase Testing every shape against every other costs O(n²) checks per frame: 1,000 colliders is about half a million pairs, almost all of them far apart. The broad phase throws away the obvious non-pairs cheaply, using only bounding boxes, so the expensive narrow-phase test runs on a handful of candidates. Quadtrees A quadtree is a tree that recursively splits 2D space. The root covers the whole world; when a node holds too many elements it is cut into four equal quadrants (NW, NE, SW, SE) and its elements move down into the child that contains them. Nodes in crowded areas keep splitting, empty areas stay as big cheap nodes. An element that straddles a split line fits no single quadrant, so it stays in the parent. Two things follow. A query ("what overlaps this rect?") skips every subtree whose quadrant does not touch the rect, so it costs roughly O(log n + k) for k results instead of O(n). And a pair search only has to compare an element with the others in its own node and in the nodes above and below it, never with distant quadrants. The price is rebuilding the tree when things move; for a moving scene the usual choice is to rebuild it every frame, which is cheap because inserts are cheap. How ASGE does it Components Velocity and Transform : position changes by velocity each frame. Collider : a Rect or Circle hitbox, independent of the sprite, with a m_Resolution of Solid (default, pushed out), Trigger (sensor, fires events, never pushed) or Unknown (ignored), plus m_Layer and m_Mask bitmasks. title: UI
text: UI Menus and HUDs in ASGE are ordinary entities with UI components, laid out and clicked by two systems. The concept Game UI has two jobs besides drawing: interaction (is the pointer over this, was it clicked) and layout (where does each widget go, so you do not position everything by hand). Treating widgets as entities means the same scene format, hierarchy and editor tooling cover UI too. Immediate versus retained UI In immediate-mode UI, code describes the interface every frame ( if (Button("Play")) ... ) and nothing persists. In retained-mode UI, widgets are objects that exist between frames, hold their own state (hovered, pressed, value) and can be saved. Game menus and HUDs, which are designed by people and loaded from files, fit retained mode. Hit testing and input states A button needs more than "mouse is over it". It has states: hovered , held and clicked . A click is conventionally registered when the button is released while still over the widget , so the player can cancel by dragging away. Overlapping widgets need a rule for which one receives the click. Layout Positioning every widget by pixel breaks when the window size or text changes. Layout containers place their children: a stack lines them up in a row or column, a grid arranges rows and columns, and absolute layout leaves positions alone. Children can ask to fill the available space or align to an edge. HUD elements are usually anchored to the screen rather than the world, so they stay put when the camera moves. How ASGE does it Widgets Each widget is a bundle of components over a UIRect : UIButton , UILabel , UICheckbox , UISlider and UIPanel . You do not assemble these by hand; the asge::game::ui::Create* functions take a descriptor and return a Result<ecs::Entity> : CreateLabel , CreateButton , CreateCheckbox , CreateSlider and CreatePanel . The editor uses the same functions, so what it builds is what a game gets. ui.cpp Copy asge::game::ui::ButtonDesc desc; desc.m_Name = "Play"; desc.m_Positi

title: Math
text: Math The small maths toolbox the rest of the engine leans on: vectors, shapes, collision tests and interpolation. The concept 2D games are mostly vectors and rectangles. Keeping them in one dependency-free module, rather than reaching into SDL types, means gameplay, physics, rendering and the editor all speak the same small set of types. Vectors A 2D vector is a pair of numbers that can mean a position, a direction or a displacement. Adding vectors moves things, a scalar multiple stretches them, and its length gives distance or speed. Working with vectors instead of separate x and y variables keeps formulas short and hard to get wrong. Shapes and overlap tests Two axis-aligned rectangles overlap exactly when they overlap on both axes, which costs a handful of comparisons. Two circles overlap when the distance between their centres is smaller than the sum of the radii. Cheap tests like these are why games approximate complicated art with simple collision shapes. Penetration Knowing that two shapes overlap is not enough to react; you also need to know how to separate them. The minimum translation vector is the shortest move that makes them just touch. For rectangles it is the smaller of the overlaps on the two axes; for circles it lies along the line between the centres. Interpolation and easing Interpolating means blending between two values by a fraction t from 0 to 1. Feeding t through an easing function makes motion start slowly, end softly or overshoot, which is what makes UI and animation feel natural. Splines extend this idea to smooth curves through several points. Floating-point rounding means tests on values should allow a small tolerance instead of exact equality. How ASGE does it Linear algebra asge::math::Vec2<T> (and Vec3 ), built on a shared VecN , with the common aliases Float2 , Double2 , Int2 and Int642 . Arithmetic operators are provided; positions, sizes and mouse deltas throughout the API are Float2 or Int2 . Geometry and collision Rect and Circle
